where: Section 1 (definition of kill[B]) and Worked example 1, step 2
problem: The text says kill[B] contains every definition in the whole flow graph of a variable that B redefines. Taken literally, that includes B's own definitions. For B1 that would give kill[B1] = {d1,d2,d3}, because B1 redefines x (d1, d3) and y (d2). Step 2 instead says kill[B1] = {d3}. A student following the definition will not get the example's set, and standard textbooks exclude a block's own definitions by putting them in gen[B].
fix: Define kill[B] as the definitions of the variables assigned in B that are not in gen[B], wherever they sit in the graph, including later blocks. In the example, B1's own definitions d1 and d2 belong to gen[B1], not kill[B1], so kill[B1] = {d3}, kill[B2] = {d1}, kill[B3] = {}. The same correction should be made in exam trap 2.

problem: The phrase 'and not killed before the end of B' describes availability at the exit of B, not at its entry, which is what IN[B] means. An expression computed on every path to B but killed inside B is still available at the entry to B, so the definition wrongly excludes it.
fix: Available at the entry of B: the expression is computed on every path from the entry of the flow graph to B, and no path kills it after its last computation on the way. Availability at the end of B is a different set, OUT[B].

where: Section 3, last paragraph, and exam trap 5
problem: 'A conservative solution keeps every fact that might be true' and 'may keep extra facts' are only correct for may analyses such as reaching definitions. For a must analysis such as available expressions, the safe answer keeps fewer facts: an expression is called available only when it is available on every path, so a conservative solution marks doubtful expressions as not available.
fix: For a may analysis, the conservative solution keeps every fact that might be true (union over all paths). For a must analysis, the conservative solution keeps only facts true on every path (intersection), so it claims fewer facts. In both cases the result is safe: it can miss an optimization but never makes the program compute a different answer.

problem: The answer's reasoning is muddled. A later definition does not stop an older definition by being 'reached from B'; rather, once control passes through B, B's assignment overrides the same variable. Because a later definition can enter B through a back edge in a loop, it can appear in IN[B] and must therefore be removed by kill[B].
fix: kill[B] must list every definition of a variable assigned in B, wherever it lies. If a definition of the same variable from a later block reaches B's entry along a loop edge, B's new assignment overrides it, so it must not appear in OUT[B]. Limiting kill to earlier definitions leaves such stale definitions in OUT[B] and gives a wrong solution.
